findings.title: Phpinfo Use
findings.description: The phpinfo() function is used to output information about PHP's configuration, which can reveal sensitive information about the environment, such as file paths and database credentials. Removing this function call prevents potential attackers from gathering this information. This fix assumes that the phpinfo() call is not necessary for the application's functionality.
findings.cwe: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
findings.fix_hint: Remove the phpinfo() function call to prevent information disclosure

<?php

define( 'DVWA_WEB_PAGE_TO_ROOT', '' );
require_once DVWA_WEB_PAGE_TO_ROOT . 'dvwa/includes/dvwaPage.inc.php';

dvwaPageStartup( array( 'authenticated') );
?>

findings.title: Tainted Sql String
findings.description: User data flows into this manually-constructed SQL string. User data can be safely inserted into SQL strings using prepared statements or an object-relational mapper (ORM). Manually-constructed SQL strings is a possible indicator of SQL injection, which could let an attacker steal or manipulate data from the database. Instead, use prepared statements (`$mysqli->prepare("INSERT INTO test(id, label) VALUES (?, ?)");`) or a safe library.
findings.cwe: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

findings.title: Echoed Request
findings.description: The original code is vulnerable to cross-site scripting attacks because it directly echoes user input. By using htmlentities(), we can ensure that any special characters in the callback function name are properly encoded, preventing malicious scripts from being injected. This fix prevents an attacker from injecting arbitrary JavaScript code by manipulating the callback parameter.
findings.cwe: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
findings.fix_hint: Use htmlentities() to sanitize the callback function name to prevent cross-site scripting vulnerabilities
findings.fixed_code: echo htmlentities($callback) . "(" . json_encode($outp) . ")";

To fix this, the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header should be set to a specific domain or a list of allowed domains. This will restrict access to only the specified domains, reducing the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks.

attack_chains.title: SQLi to RCE
attack_chains.description: An attacker uses SQL injection to extract database credentials, then uses these credentials to gain remote code execution via a tainted exec finding, achieving persistence on the system. This chain requires minimal skill and results in critical data loss. The attacker starts by exploiting a SQL injection vulnerability in the low.php file.
steps: Step 1: attacker extracts database credentials using SQL injection in vulnerabilities/sqli/source/low.php (finding 14458c81)
Step 2: attacker uses extracted credentials to gain remote code execution via a tainted exec finding in vulnerabilities/exec/source/low.php (finding f89168fd)
attack_chains.remediation: Input validation and sanitization for user-provided data in the low.php file to prevent SQL injection

attack_chains.title: Phpinfo to SQLi
attack_chains.description: An attacker uses a phpinfo finding to reveal database configuration details, then uses these details to perform a SQL injection attack, potentially extracting sensitive data. This chain requires minimal skill and results in critical data loss. The attacker starts by accessing the phpinfo.php file.
steps: Step 1: attacker reveals database configuration details using phpinfo in phpinfo.php (finding 8b2551df)
Step 2: attacker uses revealed configuration to perform SQL injection in vulnerabilities/sqli/source/low.php (finding 7b60f398)
attack_chains.remediation: Remove or restrict access to the phpinfo.php file to prevent information disclosure

attack_chains.title: Tainted Filename to RCE
attack_chains.description: An attacker uses a tainted filename finding to manipulate file paths, then uses a tainted exec finding to gain remote code execution, achieving persistence on the system. This chain requires moderate skill and results in significant data loss. The attacker starts by exploiting a tainted filename vulnerability in the instructions.php file.
steps: Step 1: attacker manipulates file paths using a tainted filename in instructions.php (finding fe7dbac4)
Step 2: attacker uses manipulated file paths to gain remote code execution via a tainted exec finding in vulnerabilities/exec/source/low.php (finding 3807f9eb)
attack_chains.remediation: Validate and sanitize user-provided filenames in the instructions.php file to prevent path manipulation

trend.message: Security posture unchanged (F) since last scan.
